progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m5-p02 (colourimeter, cuvette, absorbance, blank, A = εlc and each symbol, standards, line of best fit, read across then down, inside the standards); chem-m8-c03a (copper ammonia complex; flame test emission from excited atoms); chem-m8-p03 (qualitative: which ion); Year 11 (dilution; the visible spectrum and wavelength in nanometres, as in chem-m5-p02's 447 nm).
progression.startsWith: Two beakers of tap water look exactly the same. One holds lead above the drinking water guideline, just a few millionths of a gram in every litre. You can't see that, and no precipitate test would show so little. Now a copper solution: the deeper the blue, the more copper. Both are questions about how much, and light can answer both. So how do colour and absorption measure concentration?
progression.stopsAfter: choosing the light to measure a coloured species; explaining what a UV-visible spectrophotometer adds (one wavelength, visible or UV, a spectrum, λmax); explaining why a complex helps; calculating c from A, ε and l; explaining how AAS works and why it is specific, sensitive and limited; reading a calibration line inside its range; diluting an out-of-range sample and multiplying back by the dilution factor; choosing among colourimetry, UV-visible and AAS for a sample.

teaching.task: Two beakers of tap water look identical, but one holds lead above the drinking water guideline. A copper solution's blue gets deeper as the copper increases. How do colour and absorption turn a solution into a concentration, and which method suits which sample?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) qualitative tests say which ion; light can say how much, even when the ion is invisible (1); (2) absorbance rises with concentration (recall); a coloured species absorbs the colours it doesn't show, so measure with the light it absorbs (2); (3) UV-visible: a grating and slit pick one wavelength, visible or ultraviolet; the spectrum; measure at λmax, because the reading changes most there and a small wavelength slip changes little (3); (4) a complex absorbs more strongly, so lower concentrations read clearly; excess reagent in standards and sample alike (4); (5) A = εlc as a calculation; a calibration line is usually trusted over a book ε (5); (6) AAS: atomise in a flame, the element's own lamp, atoms absorb, light goes missing (6); (7) specific because other atoms need different energies; flame-test link; atoms, not ions; sensitive; one element per lamp; other substances matter (7); (8) calibration: standards first, blank, straight line, inside the range (8); (9) above range: dilute, don't extrapolate (9); (10) read from the line, then multiply back by the dilution factor (10); (11) choosing the technique (11); memory aid (12); attempts (13 to 16); handoff (17); key notes (18).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Two beakers of tap water look exactly the same. You met the colourimeter in Module 5. A filter lets through a whole band of colours, though. Step through the wavelengths, measuring at each, and you get an absorption spectrum. Why use the ammonia complex at all? Copper ions in water are pale blue and absorb only weakly. The law behind this is Beer-Lambert: A equals epsilon l c. Lead ions are colourless, and far too dilute for any colour test. Other atoms in the flame need different energies, so they let lead's light pass. Like the colourimeter, AAS gives absorbance, not concentration, so it needs a calibration. Here's a factory discharge tested for lead. Now read it. So which method? If the species is coloured, or can be made coloured with a complex, colourimetry is quick and cheap, and UV-visible is more selective, with one chosen wavelength. Two lines to keep. Your turn. Read point two two six across to the line and down: about two point five milligrams per litre. Last one. For the copper complex, colourimetry or UV-visible: it's strongly coloured, so it absorbs visible light, best measured at lambda max. So, to measure concentration with light, pick a method your species responds to, calibrate with standards, read inside the range, and correct for any dilution.
teaching.openingDecision: Two beakers of tap water look exactly the same. One holds lead above the drinking water guideline, just a few millionths of a gram in every litre. You can't see that, and no precipitate test would show so little. Now a copper solution: the deeper the blue, the more copper. Both are questions about how much, and light can answer both. So how do colour and absorption measure concentration?
teaching.understandingCheck: - (A1) "A sample of vineyard runoff is analysed for copper by atomic absorption spectroscopy. The calibration standards gave the results in the table, plotted on the graph. A 10.00 mL portion of the runoff was diluted to 100.0 mL with distilled water, and the diluted solution gave an absorbance of 0.226. Determine the concentration of copper in the original runoff, in mg/L." Table: copper (mg/L) 0.00, 1.00, 2.00, 3.00, 4.00; absorbance 0.000, 0.090, 0.181, 0.270, 0.361; the graph shows the points and the line of best fit. Answer: read across and down, about 2.5 mg/L (2.51 from the gradient, 0.0902 L/mg); dilution factor 100.0 ÷ 10.00 = 10.0; about 25 mg/L (25.1). Differs from the worked example in metal, range, gradient and dilution volumes; the graph read lands between gridlines. Crossed mistake: "2.5 mg/L" (the diluted value, the dilution factor lost).
